intro: Meta just dropped the biggest open-weight model to date — an 816-billion-parameter beast designed to run locally on your Mac (well, if your Mac has a terabyte of RAM) — signaling a dramatic pivot back to open AI after its recent closed-model era. But that's far from the only power move today: OpenAI is giving academic labs free access to its specialized life sciences model, Amazon unveiled wearables that passively listen and think for you, and a disturbing Citizen Lab investigation reveals how mercenary hackers hijacked ad networks to silently deliver spyware to dozens of devices. It's a day that captures AI's full spectrum — from open-source breakthroughs to invisible threats.

stories.title: Meta launches Muse Spark Open, an 816B open-weight model that runs locally on Macs
stories.summary: Meta released Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter open-weight multimodal AI model with a 1-million-token context window, developed in partnership with Apple to run locally on Apple silicon Macs using the MLX toolkit. The model is built for complex coding and agentic tasks but requires at least 1TB of RAM, running best on two M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Meta claims it is the most capable open-weight model in the US. The release signals Meta's return to open-weight AI after shifting toward closed models with its frontier Muse Wonder.
stories.opinion: A landmark moment for local inference — running an 816B model without cloud infrastructure was unthinkable recently. However, the 1TB RAM requirement limits this to a tiny audience of high-end Mac owners, and trailing Chinese open-weight competitors on coding benchmarks tempers the achievement. Where coverage differs: The Rundown AI reports Spark Open trails Chinese competitors like GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8, particularly in coding; TechCrunch reports Meta claims it is the most capable open-weight model in the US, outperforming other popular open-weight models on benchmarks

cluster.reason: Both describe Meta's launch of Muse Spark Open, the 816-billion-parameter open-weight model optimized for Apple silicon Macs.

stories.title: Mercenary hackers used targeted advertising to deliver zero-click spyware on iOS and Android
stories.summary: Citizen Lab researchers discovered a campaign dubbed AdFection in which Israeli company Discover-Tech brokered access between ad networks and mercenary spyware operators to deliver zero-click exploits via targeted ads. At least 45 devices at Al Jazeera were infected in 2024-2025, requiring no user interaction. Discover-Tech's ads appeared in over 70,000 mobile apps and 120,000 websites, reaching NATO, UN, and European government networks. Google, IAB Europe, and Beeswax have since removed Discover-Tech from their platforms.
stories.opinion: This reveals a deeply alarming attack surface: the programmatic ad ecosystem, already opaque and difficult to police, being weaponized for state-level surveillance. The sheer reach — 70,000 apps, 120,000 websites — suggests the actual infection count may far exceed what Citizen Lab has documented.

stories.title: HR Dive weekly roundup: Workers would spend up to $2,500 on career training
stories.summary: HR Dive's weekly roundup highlights five key numbers: Walmart will offer 12 weeks of paid NICU leave; only about 30% of employers track worker skills; most workers would spend a maximum of $2,500 on training for a new career; robots are cost-competitive in roughly 300,000 jobs; and a jury awarded $400,000 in compensatory damages to a former SHRM applicant denied a service dog accommodation under the ADA.
stories.opinion: The $2,500 training figure stands out as a reality check for reskilling initiatives — if workers are only willing to invest modestly in their own transitions, employer-funded programs and subsidies become even more critical in the AI displacement era.

stories.title: OpenAI offers free GPT-Rosalind access to academic research labs
stories.summary: OpenAI announced the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible academic research labs up to 30 Business Standard seats at no cost for up to 12 months with access to GPT-Rosalind, a specialized life sciences AI model. GPT-Rosalind combines frontier reasoning with a 'Rosalind workbench' for tool orchestration across medicinal chemistry, genomics, wet-lab assistance, and other scientific applications. Labs at UCSF and elsewhere are already using it for drug parameter gathering, literature exploration, experiment refinement, and protein design workflows.
stories.opinion: A smart strategic move — seeding academic labs with free access builds both goodwill and dependency. The specialized workbench approach for life sciences is more compelling than general-purpose models for this audience, though the 12-month limit raises questions about what happens to ongoing research when the free period ends.

stories.title: Turkish police raid critical TV news channel Halk TV, halting broadcasts
stories.summary: Turkish police raided the headquarters of Halk TV, one of the few Turkish news channels critical of President Erdoğan, halting live broadcasts and appointing a government administrator. The government cites financial crimes involving the network's chairman, but critics view it as suppression of dissent. A 2024 Pew Research Center survey found 91% of Turkish adults believe media should report without government censorship, yet about half said Turkish media are not very free.
stories.opinion: The Halk TV raid follows a well-established playbook of using financial allegations to justify crackdowns on critical media. The stark contrast between public support for press freedom and the reality of government control underscores the erosion of democratic norms.

stories.title: Cal AI hit $30M revenue in two years through aggressive influencer marketing
stories.summary: Cal AI, an AI calorie tracking app founded by 19-year-old Zach Yadegari in 2024, achieved over $30 million in revenue in two years through a large-scale influencer marketing strategy using college students paid on performance-based rates. The app was acquired by MyFitnessPal in March 2026. Yadegari shared these details at TechCrunch Disrupt and announced his new venture Persona, an AI agent startup that has raised $10 million to build a personal AI assistant across multiple platforms.
stories.opinion: Cal AI is a compelling case study in growth hacking rather than AI innovation — the real story is the influencer playbook, not the technology. Yadegari's pivot to an AI agent startup with Persona suggests he sees the calorie app as a stepping stone rather than a destination.

stories.title: ChatGPT Chrome extension can now read and interact with open browser tabs
stories.summary: OpenAI updated its ChatGPT Chrome extension to allow ChatGPT to view and interact with users' open browser tabs. Users can tag Chrome in the web or desktop app to have the AI read tab contents for tasks like product comparison, form filling, and email drafting. For ChatGPT Work users, the extension can actively control Chrome tabs to send messages and download files. The update comes after OpenAI discontinued its standalone ChatGPT Atlas browser.
stories.opinion: This is a significant expansion of ChatGPT's surface area into users' daily browsing, and the privacy implications are substantial — reading all open tabs means potential exposure of sensitive financial, medical, or personal data. The work-tier active control features especially blur the line between assistant and autonomous agent.

stories.title: The Guardian asks readers about using AI for online dating
stories.summary: The Guardian is soliciting reader experiences about using AI tools to assist with online dating, including generating conversation starters, profile writing, and social coaching.
stories.opinion: More of a reader engagement exercise than a news story, but it signals growing mainstream awareness and normalization of AI-assisted social interaction.

stories.title: Employee well-being improves but financial pressures drive workers to skip medical care
stories.summary: A WTW report finds employee well-being has improved since 2019, with 64% of workers saying they are physically thriving — up 10%. However, financial pressures are causing many to delay or skip medical care, with 41% of people in their 40s and 21% of employees 60 and older avoiding doctor appointments due to cost. Experts recommend employers address this through more affordable coverage, co-pay plans with consolidated billing, and assessing risk tolerance for high-cost claims.
stories.opinion: The headline improvement in well-being masks a troubling undercurrent: workers in their 40s — typically peak earning years — are skipping care at alarming rates, suggesting cost-shifting in employer plans is creating a false economy that could lead to more expensive downstream health crises.

stories.title: OpenAI launches AI for Educators course in Brazilian Portuguese on Teachers' Day
stories.summary: OpenAI announced the launch of its AI for Educators course in Brazilian Portuguese on OpenAI Academy to celebrate Teachers' Day. The course covers using AI for lesson planning, creating activities and assessments, and preparing communications. The announcement also highlights Study Mode in ChatGPT, a feature that guides students through subjects using questions, hints, and comprehension checks rather than providing direct answers.
stories.opinion: A smart localization play for a massive market — Brazil has over 2.5 million teachers. The Study Mode feature represents the more responsible side of AI in education, though its effectiveness compared to simply asking ChatGPT for answers depends heavily on student willingness to opt into the slower guided learning path.

stories.title: Sega pulls Total War: Shogun 2 remaster after backlash over AI-upscaled artwork and bugs
stories.summary: Sega pulled Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition from sale after overwhelmingly negative Steam reviews. The remaster, developed with partner studio Mataboo, promised improved visuals and UI scaling but delivered bugs and artwork that users identified as poorly upscaled using AI. Sega and Creative Assembly acknowledged the game fell short of expectations and committed to reinstating the original game and fixing the issues.
stories.opinion: A cautionary tale for the gaming industry's rush to use AI for cost-cutting on remasters. Players can clearly detect low-effort AI upscaling, and the reputational damage to a beloved franchise likely exceeds whatever was saved on art production costs.

stories.title: AI surveillance tools expand workplace monitoring beyond traditional 'bossware'
stories.summary: The Guardian reports on the growing use of AI-powered surveillance tools in workplaces that go beyond earlier 'bossware' monitoring software. These AI systems can process large volumes of data to provide detailed, minute-by-minute tracking of worker activity and productivity. The piece features UK technology editor Robert Booth discussing which sectors are adopting AI surveillance, the motivations behind it, and how such monitoring could prove counterproductive.
stories.opinion: The evolution from simple screen-capture bossware to AI-driven behavioral analytics represents a qualitative shift in workplace power dynamics. Research consistently shows that heavy monitoring undermines the trust and autonomy that drive creative and knowledge work productivity.

stories.title: Walmart expands healthcare benefits with free prescriptions, paid NICU leave, and rare disease coverage
stories.summary: Walmart announced expanded healthcare benefits including free prescriptions for over 250 medications (including GLP-1s for type 2 diabetes), 12 weeks of paid NICU leave starting November 17, and a new rare conditions center of excellence providing free specialist access through Mayo Clinic and Cleveland Clinic for conditions like MS, Parkinson's, and ALS. Premiums are increasing $1.50 per pay period to $39.80 on the starting plan, amid broader industry trends of nearly double-digit health insurance cost increases.
stories.opinion: The GLP-1 inclusion is the standout detail — while most employers are trying to limit access to these expensive drugs, Walmart is offering them free for diabetes patients. The rare disease center of excellence through Mayo and Cleveland Clinic is genuinely differentiated for a retail employer. The modest premium increase positions Walmart favorably against peers shifting costs more aggressively.

stories.title: Amazon unveils 'Bee' wearable devices for passive AI-powered ambient computing
stories.summary: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay outlined a vision for ambient AI computing at TechCrunch Disrupt, where devices work passively in the background using sensors and AI to anticipate user needs. Amazon launched new 'Bee' wearable devices — a wrist band/pendant and a magnetic smartphone attachment — that passively record audio, extract to-dos and insights in real time, then delete the raw audio. Transcripts are encrypted with user-controlled keys. Panay predicted a generational shift toward technology that automatically understands needs rather than requiring users to open specific apps.
stories.opinion: Amazon is making another bet on ambient computing after Alexa's middling results, but this time with wearables that record everything around you. The privacy design — deleting raw audio and encrypting transcripts — is the right approach, though consumer willingness to wear always-on microphones remains the fundamental barrier, not the technology.

stories.title: Hollywood releases wave of films taking aim at Silicon Valley leaders
stories.summary: The Verge reports that 2026 has seen an unusual surge of Hollywood films critically examining Big Tech, including Aaron Sorkin's 'The Social Reckoning' portraying Zuckerberg as destabilizing, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's 'You Can See Everything' on Elizabeth Holmes facing prison, Alex Gibney's 'Musk' documentary reflecting shifted public opinion, and Luca Guadagnino's 'Artificial,' a dark comedy about Sam Altman. The article frames this cluster as evidence that the tech backlash has moved from online discourse into mainstream theatrical filmmaking.
stories.opinion: Four major productions targeting four different tech figures in a single year is unprecedented and signals that filmmakers see audience appetite for tech-critical narratives. The Altman film is particularly notable given that AI is still in its ascendant phase — usually Hollywood waits for a fall before dramatizing it.

tweet_headlines.source_text:
This might be one of the most useful tools for anyone building with AI right now.

diagram-design (54k stars) is a skill for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. Point it at a repo or a website, or just describe a system, and you get a clean diagram. 44 types, all in one HTML file.

A diagram is the fastest way to understand how something works. How I’d use it:

> ask the agent to draw its plan before it writes code, and you catch a wrong architecture in 10 seconds
> hand it a repo you don’t know and see how it fits together in one picture
> map your own agent setup: where data flows, which tools run, where you approve
> READMEs people can actually read

Btw, the diagram of the repo below was made with this skill.

Same prompt, same files, two or three runs each, and a score you actually write down.

When it's just you, each job should go to the model that won it on your work, not on a chart. The method is in the image, the rest of the setup is in the article.

tweet_headlines.headline: A solo dev's full Claude Code setup: __Opus plans, Sonnet builds__, Haiku subagents for every lookup, a critic before every merge — almost all free config you set up once.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
claude code basically runs my repo now, i just review and press enter...

here's why: almost all of it is free config you set up once on day 1.

here's my whole setup and what it costs:

required (ships with claude code)

> memory → CLAUDE.md
> models → opusplan (opus plans, sonnet builds)
> search → haiku subagents for every file lookup
> review → a critic subagent before every merge
> safety → permissions in settings.json
> undo → plan mode + /rewind
> context → /clear between unrelated tasks

optional (add when you need it)

> automation → hooks that format on every write
> repeatable → skills for the prompts you retype
> parallel → git worktrees
> research → /deep-research
> escalation → an opus advisor when you're stuck
> scheduling → /schedule routines

the only thing on this list you need to pay for is your claude plan. everything else is included with claude code.

tweet_headlines.author: mardehaym
tweet_headlines.headline: The bottleneck in the agentic dev lifecycle isn't writing code anymore — it's holding __senior-engineer quality on security patches__, as LimestoneHQ's pipeline shows.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
The software development lifecycle (SDLC) is transforming into the ADLC: the agentic development lifecycle.

But that doesn’t mean the ADLC is a shorter loop.

The bottleneck shifted. Writing code got cheap. 

Holding senior-engineer quality on every change didn’t, and the hardest change to get right is the security patch.

For routine tickets, our agent pipeline at @LimestoneHQ  runs like this:

1. An engineer writes the ticket with clear acceptance criteria. Security patches and dependency upgrades come in the same way.
2. The agent proposes a plan: files, approach, risks.
3. An engineer approves the plan.
4. The agent builds in a sandbox that can reach the model and nothing else.
5. CI runs the same checks on every change, and the agent fixes what fails.
6. An engineer reviews the PR. Nothing reaches main without that approval.
7. Approved review feedback becomes a rule for the next run.

Agents write the code. Engineers approve it.

- Long-context window management

- Chaining (Deterministic flows)
- Routing (Selecting the right model for the task)

- Tool Use (Search, APIs, Code Interpreters)

- Golden Datasets (Establishing Ground Truth)
- LLM-as-a-Judge (Using strong models to grade weak ones)
- Metrics: Faithfulness, Answer Relevance, Recall
- Continuous Eval in CI/CD pipelines

6. Ops & Monitoring:

- Tracing (Debugging the chain)
- Cost & Latency optimization

tweet_headlines.author: daniel_mac8
tweet_headlines.headline: Claude Code's desktop app lands __nested sessions and a /btw side-tab__ among seven new features — parallel work without losing your main thread.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
🌟 Claude Code on the desktop got a serious glow up. It's honestly way better.

Try these 7 new features:

1. Saved environments: save a few folders, an SSH host, or cloud as one setup and start sessions there

2. A worktree per folder, so parallel sessions don't step on each other

3. Nested sessions: ask for parallel tasks and each one reports back to the main thread

4. /btw (Cmd+;): side questions open in their own tab while the main session keeps working

5. One-click follow-ups: Claude suggests the next task, one click runs it as its own session

6. Sidebar status: see which sessions are working and which need you

7. Recap cards + a live to-do list, so you can catch up on a session in seconds

The new /btw is probably my favorite. Hard to say, these all sound great. How about you? https://t.co/TLbBpi3klq

human_items.headline: HR Dive weekly roundup: Workers would spend up to $2,500 on career training
human_items.summary: HR Dive's weekly roundup highlights five key numbers: Walmart will offer 12 weeks of paid NICU leave; only about 30% of employers track worker skills; most workers would spend a maximum of $2,500 on training for a new career; robots are cost-competitive in roughly 300,000 jobs; and a jury awarded $400,000 in compensatory damages to a former SHRM applicant denied a service dog accommodation under the ADA.
human_items.meaning: Be explicit about whose work changes and what happens to the people doing it.

human_items.headline: AI surveillance tools expand workplace monitoring beyond traditional 'bossware'
human_items.summary: The Guardian reports on the growing use of AI-powered surveillance tools in workplaces that go beyond earlier 'bossware' monitoring software. These AI systems can process large volumes of data to provide detailed, minute-by-minute tracking of worker activity and productivity. The piece features UK technology editor Robert Booth discussing which sectors are adopting AI surveillance, the motivations behind it, and how such monitoring could prove counterproductive.
human_items.meaning: Decide the boundary before the tool is in daily use.

human_items.headline: Employee well-being improves but financial pressures drive workers to skip medical care
human_items.summary: A WTW report finds employee well-being has improved since 2019, with 64% of workers saying they are physically thriving — up 10%. However, financial pressures are causing many to delay or skip medical care, with 41% of people in their 40s and 21% of employees 60 and older avoiding doctor appointments due to cost. Experts recommend employers address this through more affordable coverage, co-pay plans with consolidated billing, and assessing risk tolerance for high-cost claims.
human_items.meaning: Be explicit about whose work changes and what happens to the people doing it.
